These droplets gather together and fall down as rain. The sun warms the earth, and that warm air rises again, which makes the whole process start all over.

So, no one turns the rain on like a faucet. It’s just nature’s way of keeping our planet healthy and clean. When rain falls, it soaks into the ground, fills up rivers, and helps plants grow. It’s a natural part of life, even if it feels frustrating when you’re looking forward to playing outside.

If you’re feeling upset about missing recess, you could try drawing a picture of the rain, reading a book, or playing a quiet game with a friend. The sun will come back out soon, and you’ll have plenty of time to play when the ground is dry again.

prompt: When it’s cold waiting for the bus, I get tiny bumps on my arms. Why do we get goosebumps?

Here's what's going on: Your body has tiny muscles under your skin called arrector pili muscles. When it gets cold, or when you're feeling strong emotions like excitement or fear, these muscles squeeze the hair follicles on your skin. That makes the bumps appear, and it can also make your hair stand up a little.

Goosebumps are a bit like a reflex — your body does it automatically without you thinking about it. They used to help our ancestors when they were scared, because the bumps made their body look bigger and scarier to predators. But now they mostly just happen when we're cold or surprised.

So when you're waiting for the bus on a cold morning, your body is just trying to keep you warm by making those little bumps. It's totally normal and nothing to worry about. You can even try it on purpose — take a cold shower or hold a cold drink, and you'll see those bumps appear!
